# The producer's own overlap rule decides who gets the claim

A claim producer that advertises the scopes-conflict capability defines what
"overlapping" means for its own store. Two scopes can be byte-unequal and still
overlap. Rimsky asks the producer, and refuses the second writer when the
producer says they overlap — on the ordinary claim path and on the fan-out
sub-claim path alike.

## The deployment

```yaml
persistence:
  driver: sqlite
  sqlite:
    path: /var/lib/rimsky/state.db
claim_producers:
  "overlap-store":
    endpoint: "grpc://overlap-store:9461"
    write_semantics_allowed: ["sync"]
named_locks: {}
executors: {}
```

The producer used below defines overlap as "the two selectors end in the same
path segment", so `/west/reports` and `/east/reports` overlap while
`/west/reports` and `/east/invoices` do not.

## Hold a scope durably

```yaml
name: overlap-owner
version: v1
nodes:
  - type: owner
    executor: http-node
    claim_producers:
      - name: overlap-store
        selector: "{{params.selector}}"
        intent: rw
        alias: held
        lifetime: durable
    error_types:
      "acquire/unavailable": {action: give_up}
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          url:       {type: string, default: "http://recorder:19459/rec/owner"}
          method:    {type: string, default: POST}
          held_addr: {type: string, source: "{{claim.held.address}}"}
```

```bash
rimsky instance create "$OWNER_TPL" --params '{"selector":"/west/reports"}' \
  --endpoint "$BASE" -o json
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/observability/claim-handles?limit=200"
```

The owning node settles fresh. Its claim handle reads `lifetime: durable` and
`state: committed`, so the scope stays occupied after the node settles.

## An overlapping scope is refused

```yaml
name: overlap-competitor
version: v1
nodes:
  - type: competitor
    executor: http-node
    claim_producers:
      - name: overlap-store
        selector: "{{params.selector}}"
        intent: rw
        alias: held
    error_types:
      "acquire/unavailable": {action: give_up}
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          url:       {type: string, default: "http://recorder:19459/rec/competitor"}
          method:    {type: string, default: POST}
          held_addr: {type: string, source: "{{claim.held.address}}"}
```

```bash
rimsky instance create "$COMPETITOR_TPL" --params '{"selector":"/east/reports"}' \
  --endpoint "$BASE" -o json
```

`/east/reports` is byte-unequal to the held scope and is neither a prefix nor a
suffix of it. Rimsky puts the pair to the producer, the producer answers that
they overlap, and the node settles
`terminal/error/acquire/unavailable`. The two writers cannot both hold claims.

## A non-overlapping scope is claimed straight away

```bash
rimsky instance create "$COMPETITOR_TPL" --params '{"selector":"/east/invoices"}' \
  --endpoint "$BASE" -o json
```

This one settles fresh with its claim. The rule discriminates rather than
refusing everything.

## The same rule governs fan-out sub-claims

```yaml
name: overlap-fanout
version: v1
nodes:
  - type: partitioned
    executor: http-node
    claim_producers:
      - name: overlap-store
        selector: /inbox
        intent: rw
        alias: parent
    error_types:
      "acquire/unavailable": {action: give_up}
    fan_out:
      claim: parent
      partition_request: '{"list": [{"key": "a/p1"}, {"key": "b/p1"}]}'
      parallelism: 2
      error_policy:
        kind: strict
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          url:       {type: string, default: "http://recorder:19459/rec/partitioned"}
          method:    {type: string, default: POST}
          partition: {type: string, source: "{{child.partition_key}}"}
          held_addr: {type: string, source: "{{claim.parent.address}}"}
```

The two sub-claims `/inbox/a/p1` and `/inbox/b/p1` are byte-unequal and
overlapping under this producer's rule. Rimsky puts that pair to the producer on
the fan-out path too, and the producer calls them overlapping. Neither sub-claim
gets a claim handle and the fan-out settles neither partition.

The no-overlapping-writers rule holds where an operator is most likely to
generate overlapping scopes by accident, not only on claims a template names one
at a time.
